The University of Sharjah offers on-campus housing for male and female students, providing a comfortable, supportive environment that fosters academic success and social interaction. The dormitories are managed by experienced supervisors who take care of the students’ needs, both local and international.
The Men's Dormitory offers a range of room types, from deluxe to standard, to ensure that every student’s needs are met. The goal is to provide a comfortable environment for academic achievement and cultural exchange among students from diverse backgrounds.
Mens Dorm/Housing Room Types: Single Deluxe Room: Private room with a kitchen and bathroom. Single Standard Room: Private room with shared kitchen and bathroom. Double Deluxe Room: Shared room for two with a kitchen and bathroom. Double Standard Room: Shared room for two with a shared kitchen and bathroom (for four people). Triple Room: Room for three students with a shared external kitchen and bathroom.
Mens Dorm/Housing Main Tasks of Dormitory Staff: 1.Welcoming and guiding new residents. 2.Informing students about housing rules and regulations. 3.Organizing recreational activities and weekly shopping trips. 4.Providing advice and support to residents. 5.Ensuring the rooms are fully equipped and well-maintained.
Mens Dorm/Housing Facilities & Services: Weekly shopping trips. Furnishing, cleaning, and room maintenance. Computer lab and printers. TV viewing rooms. High-speed internet and room connectivity. 24/7 healthcare and security.
Mens Dorm/Housing Housing Fees & Payment Information: A AED 1000 deposit is required, refundable at check-out if no damage occurs. 25% of the room fee is paid upfront, with the remainder paid during the semester. Non-refundable advance: The 25% payment is non-refundable if the student withdraws. Withdrawal fees: 25% of the fees if withdrawn in the first month, 50% if withdrawn in the second month, and no refund after two months.
Mens Dorm/Housing Special Note:Postgraduate, master’s, and training students (except teaching assistants) pay an additional 50% of the room fee.
Mens Dorm/Housing Room Fee Rates: Room Type	Semester Fee (AED)	Summer Fee (AED) => Single Special	6,493	3,004 , Single Normal	5,544	2,144 , Double Special	3,183	1,482 , Double Normal	2,356	1,095 , Triple	1,885	870
Mens Dorm/Housing Prohibited Actions:Smoking. Damaging property. Disrupting peace. Unauthorized overnight stays or visitors. Bringing animals or children.
Women’s Dormitory: The Women’s Dormitory at UoS is designed to provide a home-like environment where female students can thrive academically and socially. The dormitory includes comfortable lounges, study halls, computer labs, and entertainment facilities like TV lounges and free Wi-Fi.
Women’s Dorm/Housing Key Features: Psychosocial Support: Counseling and guidance on academic, social, and health-related matters., Recreational Activities: Weekly outings, sports events, and fun programs., Supervision: 24-hour supervision to ensure students’ safety and well-being.
Women’s Dorm/Housing Dormitory Locations: General Dormitories: Located near the student center (8 buildings)., Medical College Dormitories: Dedicated housing for medical students (5 buildings).
Women’s Dorm/Housing Accommodation Process: Students and their guardians must present essential documents for registration., The student’s preferences and room availability will be considered during placement.
Women’s Dorm/Housing Policies & Procedures: New students are welcomed, briefed on rules, and provided with housing assignments., Special care is given to students with medical or personal needs., The dormitory fosters an environment of support, creativity, and academic excellence.

Health and Wellness at the University of Sharjah: At the University of Sharjah, we prioritize both your physical and mental well-being, offering a variety of services to support students in every aspect of their health.
Healthcare Services: Our 24-hour medical clinics and ambulance services ensure that healthcare is always within reach. Equipped with state-of-the-art facilities, the clinics cater to both male and female students. Additionally, we provide cutting-edge dental hospital services on campus for comprehensive healthcare support.
Health and Wellness Entertainment & Social Life: Immerse yourself in the vibrant university experience with numerous events and activities, such as cultural celebrations, student excursions, theater productions, concerts, festivals, and awareness days like Biodiversity and Cancer Awareness days. These events enrich your university life and create lasting memories.
Health and Wellness Psychological Counseling: Mental health is just as important as physical health at UoS. Our Psychological Support and Counseling team offers a range of services for students, staff, faculty, and parents, including individual and group counseling, psychoeducational workshops, crisis intervention, and psychological assessments. We adopt a short-term, solution-focused approach, typically spanning 8 to 10 sessions, and provide extended interventions when needed to help you navigate personal, family, and work-related challenges.
Health and Wellness Disability Resource Center: In collaboration with Sharjah City for Humanitarian Services (SCHS), we have established the Disability Resource Center to provide tailored academic assistance and extracurricular activities. We aim to create an inclusive environment where students with disabilities have the support and resources needed to excel.
Health and Wellness Hair & Beauty Salons: Stay fresh and maintain your style with our on-campus barbershops and hair salons, available for both men and women. These convenient facilities allow you to look your best without ever leaving campus.
Sports at the University of Sharjah: At UoS, sports are an essential part of student life, offering more than just physical activity. Sports at UoS are also about fostering camaraderie, community, and lifelong memories.
Sports Complexes: Our main campus features two top-tier sports complexes—one for men and one for women. Each complex offers a range of facilities, including Olympic-size swimming pools, versatile indoor sports halls, and fully equipped gymnasiums. Whether you're into bodybuilding, basketball, volleyball, or yoga, you'll find the ideal space to engage in your favorite sport. We also offer specialized training for faculty, staff, and their children in swimming, karate, and physical fitness, all led by expert trainers.
Sports Teams: At UoS, we have dynamic sports teams that cater to both men and women, providing opportunities for all levels of athletes. Whether you're a seasoned competitor or new to the game, our teams offer the perfect blend of competition and instruction. Participate in intramural and extramural tournaments to showcase your skills, make lasting connections, and be part of our spirited athletic community.
Sports Gallery: Explore the excitement of our sports events and teams through our gallery, where you can see highlights from competitions and team activities.

Student Council: The Students' Advisory Council at the University of Sharjah (UoS) is an elected body of students dedicated to representing the interests of the student body. The council works collaboratively with university administration to help foster a supportive and dynamic university environment that promotes student services, growth, and well-being.
Objectives of the Student Council: Strengthening Cooperation and Teamwork: Foster a sense of unity and teamwork among students, while enhancing the relationship between students and university staff and faculty., Developing Leadership Skills: Provide students with opportunities to develop leadership skills and express their opinions and needs in a constructive manner., Providing Input on University Decisions: Offer valuable feedback on decisions related to academic, administrative, and student services matters at UoS., Addressing Student Issues: Collaborate with relevant departments to resolve academic, social, and behavioral challenges faced by students., Supporting Academic Achievement: Encourage students' academic progress and assist in providing support for academic success., Enhancing Student Activities: Promote and support student engagement in academic, cultural, social, and sports activities, as well as volunteer work programs., Raising Awareness of Rights and Responsibilities: Educate students about their rights and responsibilities within the framework of university regulations., Proposing Initiatives for Development: Submit proposals for the enhancement of plans, regulations, procedures, and activities.
Student Council's Role: Expressing Student Opinions: The council provides a platform for students to voice their opinions on university matters and ensures their concerns are heard., Enhancing Services: Actively seeks opportunities to improve student services, aiming to enrich the overall student experience., Defending Student Interests: Represents student perspectives to the university administration and relevant stakeholders., Launching Leadership Programs: Initiates projects that help students develop leadership skills and promote teamwork., Promoting Student Well-being: Focuses on addressing students’ academic, social, and personal needs to ensure their overall well-being., Informing the Community: Plays an essential role in keeping the university community informed about key events, announcements, and updates.

University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) Welcome Message: As the Director of UDHS, it gives me great pleasure to welcome you to the University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS). The Hospital was opened on June 11, 2011, and since then many things have changed over the years, with more improvements expected in the future. In addition to the teaching clinics for undergraduate and postgraduate dental students, UDHS also provides a training program for interns, as well as a Center of Excellence where our highly qualified academics provide their expertise to the community.UDHS strives to be recognized internationally as a contemporary, progressive, innovative, and vibrant center for dental education and patient service. Our mission is to achieve distinction in dental education, research, and oral health care to the benefit of our local community. UDHS continually works towards enhancing the learning experience of our students. We aim to ensure that all our students are able to succeed and thrive not only in their studies but also in their future dental careers.Student education is achieved through the interaction of dedicated, highly qualified academics and tutors, in state-of-the-art facilities, with up-to-date equipment and technology. UDHS offers a full range of general and specialty dental services to the Sharjah community, and we are proud of the high standard of care provided by our hospital. UDHS is well connected with alumni, the community, and the profession, fostering strong relationships and continuous development. Dr. Wael TalaatActing Director of University Dental Hospital Sharjah
University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) The Center of Excellence for Dental Medicine at the University of Sharjah. The Center of Excellence for Dental Medicine is a prestigious facility within the University Dental Hospital Sharjah, dedicated to providing high-quality oral healthcare. As an integral part of the University of Sharjah, the center upholds the institution’s commitment to excellence in education, research, and clinical practice. It aims to deliver top-tier dental care using state-of-the-art technology, facilitated by highly qualified clinicians with specialized expertise.
University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) Advanced Facilities and Specialized Care : The center is equipped with six modern dental clinics, each integrated with cutting-edge technology. One of its unique features is an interactive multimedia system embedded within the dental chairs. This system helps patients understand their treatment plans and available alternatives, ensuring informed decision-making. The center brings together a variety of dental specialties under one roof, fostering a multidisciplinary approach to patient care. This structure allows for the comprehensive treatment of both common and complex dental and oro-facial conditions.. For cases that require more advanced interventions, the center’s specialists also perform complex surgical procedures. When necessary, holistic dental care is provided under general anesthesia at the neighboring University Hospital Sharjah, particularly for young children who may be uncooperative during procedures under local anesthesia.
University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) Range of Specialized Services. The center offers a wide range of dental procedures tailored to meet the diverse needs of patients. These include: . Restorative and Aesthetic Dentistry – Enhancing dental function and aesthetics through advanced restorative techniques. . General Dentistry – Comprehensive dental care for overall oral health maintenance. . Pediatric Dentistry – Specialized dental care for children, ensuring early diagnosis and treatment. . Periodontal Treatment – Treatment of gum diseases and other periodontal conditions. . Orthodontic Treatment – Correction of dental misalignment using braces and aligners. . Cosmetic and Laser Dentistry – Advanced aesthetic procedures, including laser treatments. . Minor Oral Surgery and Dental Implants – Surgical procedures for tooth extractions, implants, and more. . Orthognathic and Major Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery – Surgical treatment for jaw and facial abnormalities. . Oral Medicine and Oro-facial Pain Management – Diagnosis and treatment of complex oral diseases and pain disorders. . Temporo-mandibular Joint Disorders (TMJ) – Specialized care for jaw joint dysfunctions. . People of Determination Clinic – Tailored dental care for individuals with special needs. . Operating Hours and Accessibility . The Center of Excellence for Dental Medicine operates from Monday to Thursday, from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM. It remains closed on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays. The center is also committed to accessibility, providing sign language services to ensure inclusive healthcare for all patients.

University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) The Center of Excellence for Dental Medicine at the University of Sharjah stands as a beacon of innovation and quality in the field of dentistry. Through its comprehensive range of services, advanced technology, and highly skilled specialists, the center continues to set benchmarks in dental education, research, and patient care.
Teaching Clinics at the University Dental Hospital Sharjah: The Teaching Clinics at the University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) play a vital role in both patient care and dental education. As an integral part of the College of Dental Medicine, these clinics provide a hands-on learning environment for student doctors while delivering high-quality dental treatments to the community. Under the close supervision of experienced faculty members, students gain practical experience in diagnosing and treating a wide range of dental conditions.
Teaching-Clinics: Comprehensive Dental Treatment Under Supervision: A significant portion of the UDHS facility is dedicated to teaching clinics, where patients receive treatment from dental students following a thorough diagnostic process. This process includes:
Teaching-Clinics: A complete medical history review. Mucosal examination . Radiological assessment .Patients undergo a structured and pre-approved treatment plan that covers restorative dentistry, prosthodontics, and surgical procedures. To ensure quality care, students work in pairs and have access to all the necessary instruments and materials. Every step of the procedure is monitored and approved by the attending faculty members, who specialize in various fields of dentistry.
Teaching-Clinics: Patient Eligibility and Care Process: Patients eligible for treatment within the Teaching Clinics are placed on a waiting list and contacted once their treatment plan is ready. The clinics adhere to strict infection control policies and quality assurance standards, ensuring patient safety and comfort. Additionally, Patients' Rights and Responsibilities are respected at all times, reinforcing a patient-centered approach to care.
Teaching-Clinics: Commitment to Excellence in Dental Education: UDHS continuously strives to enhance both the quality of care provided to patients and the educational experience of its students. By integrating patient care into the dental curriculum, the Teaching Clinics serve as a bridge between theoretical knowledge and real-world clinical practice. This hands-on training is crucial for preparing future dental professionals to deliver exceptional care.
Teaching-Clinics: Specialized Clinics within the Teaching Facility: The Teaching Clinics at UDHS encompass multiple specialized units, ensuring a wide range of dental care services: 1. Urgent Care Clinic – Provides immediate dental treatment for emergency cases. 1. General Practice Clinics – Focuses on routine dental care and treatment planning. 1. Internship Clinic – A training ground for dental interns transitioning into professional practice. 1. Postgraduate Dental Center – Offers advanced training and treatment by postgraduate students under expert supervision. 1. Through these specialized clinics, the University Dental Hospital Sharjah continues to uphold its mission of delivering top-tier dental education while making quality dental care accessible to the community.
URGENT-CARE-CLINIC: Urgent Care Clinic at the University Dental Hospital Sharjah: The Urgent Care Clinic at the University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS) is a dedicated walk-in facility that provides immediate dental care for both new and previously registered patients. Designed to address dental emergencies, the clinic ensures that patients experiencing severe discomfort or urgent dental conditions receive prompt medical attention.
URGENT-CARE-CLINIC: Services Offered: The clinic offers a range of emergency dental treatments, including but not limited to: 1. Initial Dental Screening – A quick assessment of the patient's condition. 1. Treatment for Dental Trauma – Immediate care for injuries affecting the teeth, gums, and surrounding tissues. 1. Management of Uncontrolled Dental Bleeding – Urgent intervention for excessive bleeding. 1. Treatment of Rapidly Increasing Facial Infections and Swellings – Immediate attention to infections that pose a risk to oral and general health. 1. Relief for Severe Dental and Facial Pain – Management of extreme pain that cannot be controlled by over-the-counter medications.
URGENT-CARE-CLINIC: Treatment Process and Admission Criteria. The Urgent Care Clinic is managed by intern doctors (graduate dentists) under the supervision of licensed professionals. Patients must meet the following criteria to be admitted for urgent care: 1. Require emergency dental treatment for a qualifying condition. 1. Hold a valid UAE residency visa to access services. 1. Have a medical file at UDHS (if not, a new file will be opened upon arrival). .Upon arrival, patients undergo a triage evaluation, where a doctor assesses their condition and directs them to the appropriate clinic for treatment.
URGENT-CARE-CLINIC: Waiting Time and Treatment Continuation. Due to the high volume of daily patients, waiting times may vary. Once admitted, the primary goal is to evaluate and stabilize the urgent condition. Following stabilization, patients have the option to:. 1. Continue their full treatment at UDHS – Their name will be added to the waiting list for further dental procedures. 1. Seek treatment elsewhere – Patients are free to continue their care at another dental facility.
General Practice Clinics at the University Dental Hospital Sharjah (UDHS): The General Practice Clinics at UDHS provide comprehensive dental care while serving as a hands-on training facility for dental students. These clinics cover various aspects of general and specialized dentistry, ensuring that patients receive high-quality treatment while students gain valuable clinical experience under expert supervision.
General Practice Clinics Comprehensive Care Clinics. These clinics adopt a Comprehensive Dental Care (CDC) approach, ensuring that students provide patient-centered care in a manner similar to actual dental practice. The focus is on: 1. Holistic patient treatment – Students create treatment plans that involve the patient in maintaining their oral health. 1. Continuous education – Ensuring that students learn patient-focused care and sensitivity. 1. Supervised training – All treatments are performed under the guidance of experienced faculty members.
General Practice Clinics Oral Medicine / Oral Diagnosis Clinic: This clinic specializes in diagnosing and treating a variety of oral diseases, including: 1. Oral ulcers and white patches (Leukoplakia)1. Lumps and salivary gland diseases1. Oral infections1. Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Disorders1. Non-dental pain conditions (e.g., burning mouth, nerve pain)
General Practice Clinics Consultation Process: 1. Patients can self-refer or be referred by another medical or dental practitioner.1. Registration at UDHS and initial screening at the Urgent Care Clinic is required.1. Consultation fees are waived, except for cases requiring lab tests, which are paid for by the patient.
General Practice Clinics Oral Surgery Clinic: Oral Surgery is a critical part of dental care, and UDHS offers specialized services in: 1. Undergraduate and Postgraduate Clinics 1. Minor Oral Surgery Teaching Clinic 1. Dental Laser Clinic 1. Dental Implant Clinic 1. TMJ Clinic
General Practice Clinics Treatments Provided: 1. Dental infection management 1. Tooth extractions (including impacted teeth removal) 1. Oral soft tissue tumor and bone lesion management 1. Dental implants for missing teeth replacement 1. Cosmetic dental laser procedures 1. Jaw joint problem treatments. All procedures are carried out by undergraduate or postgraduate students under the direct supervision of Oral & Maxillofacial Surgery specialists.
General Practice Clinics Pediatric Dentistry Clinics: This clinic provides comprehensive oral healthcare for infants, children, and adolescents, ensuring: 1. Routine dental treatments – Performed by dental students under supervision. 1. Advanced treatments for younger children – Sedation (Nitrous Oxide) or General Anesthesia is used for children who cannot cooperate. 1. Special needs dental care – Provided in a dedicated Special Needs Clinic. 1. Orthodontic treatments – To correct misaligned teeth and improve functional occlusion in children and adolescents.
General Practice Clinics People of Determination Clinic: This clinic provides routine dental care to patients with special needs, including:
General Practice Clinics Physical disabilities: 1. ental or intellectual disabilities 1. ision or hearing impairments 1. enetic disorders (e.g., syndromes) 1. sychiatric conditions 1. besity-related complications 1. ental phobias 1. nfectious diseases (Hepatitis, HIV, etc.) 1. edical conditions affecting dental treatment (e.g., prolonged bleeding) 1. eriatric conditions (e.g., dementia, Alzheimer's disease) 1. ery young patients (newborns and infants)
General Practice Clinics Admission Process: 1. Initial dental screening at the Urgent Care Clinic is required. 1. Dental care is discussed and evaluated with a specialist. 1. If further lab tests or medical reports are needed, a new appointment will be scheduled. 1. Advanced cases requiring general anesthesia are referred to the University Hospital Sharjah.
Internship Training Program Overview: The College of Dental Medicine offers a comprehensive Dental Internship Program for graduates who have completed their Bachelor of Dental Surgery. The program lasts 12 months and is divided into three core clinical rotations, each lasting four months: 1. Restorative Dentistry 2. Oral Diagnosis & Oral Surgery 3. Pedodontics, Orthodontics, and Community Dentistry This internship program provides an exciting opportunity for newly graduated dentists to gain broad-based clinical training across various dental disciplines. It prepares interns for focused career paths, supported by a rigorous educational framework that sharpens clinical skills and deepens knowledge.
Internship Training Program Accreditation: The program is reviewed and accredited by the National Institute for Health Specialties (NIHS) in the UAE, ensuring the highest standards of education and clinical training.
Internship Training Program Clinical Training Objectives: 1. The program enhances competencies in all aspects of general dentistry. 2. Interns will work on advanced, complex cases, helping them: A. Explore potential areas of interest in patient care. B. Discover or solidify fields for future postgraduate study. 3. The training ensures graduates upgrade their knowledge and acquire new skills beneficial for both patient care and professional growth. 4. It encourages self-directed learning, where interns take responsibility for their professional development, aligning their learning with patient care needs.
Internship Training Program Lifelong Learning in Dentistry: 1. Postgraduate dental education is essential to maintaining high standards of patient care.1. The College of Dental Medicine offers interns the foundation for continuous professional development.1. The commitment to lifelong learning begins during undergraduate studies and extends throughout a dentist’s career.

Mobile Dental Clinic Overview: 1. Provides oral care services to individuals who have difficulty accessing conventional dental clinics. 2. Aims to improve oral health and quality of life for the elderly and underserved populations in urban and rural areas of Sharjah.
Mobile Dental Clinic Vision and Mission: Vision: To provide oral care services to those unable to access conventional dental clinics. Mission: To improve oral health and quality of life for the elderly and underserved communities in Sharjah by bringing mobile dental care directly to them.
Mobile Dental Clinic Scope of Dental Services: 1. Professional dental cleaning. 1. Multiple fillings and extractions (excluding surgical extractions). 1. Emergency dental care for issues like dental pain or cavities, including endodontics (pulp removal) and referrals. 1. Services are provided at seven locations across the Emirate of Sharjah: Khorfakkan, Kalba, Dibba Al-Hisn, Al Madam, Al Dhaid, Al Hamriyah, and Nursing Home-Muwaileh.
Mobile Dental Clinic Operational Details: 1. The MDC operates three times a week with one full-time clinical staff member, 60 graduates (interns), and three auxiliary staff members supervised by faculty. 1. The clinic is fully equipped with three dental units, a digital X-ray facility, and a wheelchair carrier lift. 1. Meets Infection Prevention and Control standards with regular maintenance to ensure patient safety.
Mobile Dental Clinic Community Dental Service and Outreach: 1. Offers free preventive and restorative care to underserved populations, promoting optimal oral health and enhancing quality of life. 1. Provides free high-quality dental care to those who cannot afford or access dental treatments.
Mobile Dental Clinic Special Programs: 1. School Oral Health Program: Offers dental services, including classroom education, dental screenings, preventive care (sealants, fluoride varnish), and restorative care to around 100 children every year.1. Special Needs Dentistry: Provides dental health care to special needs patients, with hands-on supervised experience for students and interns to ensure effective care for this community.

University-Dental-Hospital Support Services Overview: Provides a range of services across different specialties to ensure smooth and effective dental care and operations within the hospital. Includes state-of-the-art technology, software, and support departments to enhance patient care, student education, and staff operations. 1. Oral Radiology Unit: . Serves all UDHS clinics, offering consistent service during clinic hours. . Uses the latest X-ray technologies, including a CBCT machine for 3D X-ray images and panoramic X-ray machines for 2D images. . Provides essential intra-oral X-rays with backup machines for consistent service. . Follows FANR regulations for ionizing radiation protection, ensuring safety for patients and operators. . Services are offered under the supervision of two Oral Radiology Specialists and three X-ray Technicians. 2. Electronic Health Records (axiUm): . A state-of-the-art dental academic software, first implemented in the Middle East at UDHS. . Manages patient records, student evaluations, clinical research, and financial/administrative tasks. . Enhances seamless integration between student management, course management, and patient care, ensuring high-quality evidence-based oral health services and education. 3. Dental Technology Laboratory: . Focuses on designing and manufacturing corrective dental devices and replacements for natural teeth. . Technicians collaborate with dentists to plan, design, and fabricate dental prostheses for patients. . Operates four days per week, 10 hours per day. 4. Central Sterilization Services Department (CSSD): . Responsible for cleaning, decontaminating, packaging, and sterilizing medical and surgical instruments. . Implements standardized reprocessing using washer-disinfectors and sterilizers, ensuring maximum safety and infection control. . Uses T-DOC advanced technology for scanning and tracing instruments, improving patient safety. . Staff is well-trained in risk management and quality assurance practices to ensure safety for patients and staff. . Operates Monday to Thursday, from 07:30 AM to 05:30 PM, with a team of five staff members.
Asset Transfer Guidelines: 1. Access the Asset Management System: . URL: Navigate to https://assetsms.sharjah.ac.ae or access it via MYUOSPORTAL. . To Access MYUOSPORTAL: Click Quick Links > MyUOS on the UOS website. 2. Home Page: Upon logging in, you'll be greeted with the Asset Management System's Home page. 3. Initiating Asset Transfer: . Navigate to: Transaction Menu > Asset Movement sub-menu. . Select the asset from the list that you wish to transfer. 4. Asset Transfer Request: . Transfers can be done in the following scenarios: -> Transfer to a different location. -> Transfer to a different custodian. . Details to provide: -> Select the location, custodian, or both. -> Specify the movement reason. . After filling in the details, click the ‘Move’ button to initiate the transfer, which triggers an email notification to the receiver. 5. Asset Transfer Request Success: A success popup will appear stating "Asset sent for Approval." 6. Receiver – Assets Transfer Approval: The receiver will see a notification at the top of the home page. Clicking the notification will take them to the approval screen where they can view pending transfers. 7. Receiver – Approve or Reject Transfer: . Approve: Select the asset and click ‘Approve’ to complete the transfer. . Reject: If the transfer request is invalid, select ‘Reject’, specify a reason (optional), and click Reject. 8. Approval/Reject Success: Approval: A confirmation message ‘Approve Success!!’ will appear. Rejection: A confirmation message ‘Reject Success!!’ will appear. 9. Partial Approval/Reject: The receiver can approve or reject multiple assets partially.
Please Refer for Asset Transfer Guidelines:  https://www.sharjah.ac.ae/-/media/project/uos/sites/uos/discover-uos/asset_transfer_guide.pdf

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: The University of Sharjah and the University of Malaya Sign a Memorandum of UnderstandingThe University of Sharjah has recently signed a joint memorandum of understanding withthe University of Malaya, Malaysia. The agreement aims to facilitate the granting of a doubledoctorate in selected engineering disciplines such as Electrical Engineering, EngineeringManagement, and Civil Engineering. With time, the program will expand to include MechanicalEngineering and Renewable Energy. The memorandum will enable students to obtain adoctorate degree accredited by both universities and benefit from joint-supervision. To beeligible, graduate students and researchers must meet the conditions and rules of eachuniversity

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: Architectural Engineering: AE Faculty paper featured in the Editor's Choice Selection of the Journal of Architectural Engineering: AE Faculty, Vittorino Belpoliti, Emad S. N. Mushtaha, Ahmed A. Saleem, and former chairperson Abbas A. Elmualim, published paper, Assessment of Natural Ventilation Techniques by Means of Measurements and Retrospective CFD Simulation on a Test Building, was announced as Editor ’ s Choice section of the Journal of Architectural Engineering page in the ASCE Library. It is available for free for 3 months and is being featured in the selected section in the ASCE website and ASCE's social media accounts. The study compares CFD digital simulations results and field measurement on a prototype building in the UAE. The analysis quantified 0.7°C/day indoor temperature reduction due to natural ventilation strategies
COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: Architectural Engineering: Public lecture in Vernacular Architecture and cultural heritage: The Department of Architectural Engineering hosted a public lecture by Dr. Alina Elena Voinea from the Faculty of Architecture and Urban Planning at the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania organized by Dr. Eslam Nofal. Dr. Alina is a leading researcher in the field of vernacular architecture, with a particular focus on the cultural heritage of Transylvania. Dr. Voinea's research explores the ways in which architectural forms and techniques can embody and transmit cultural identity. Her work has been published in numerous academic journals and she is a frequent speaker at international conferences

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: Civil & Environmental Engineering: "Geo-Talks" Geotechnical Seminar: On January 11th, 2024, the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering hosted the "Geo-Talks" Geotechnical Seminar at M9 - Albayrouni Hall, in collaboration with the National Marine Dredging Company (NMDC), New York University of Abu Dhabi, and ADEC Engineering Consultancy. COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: Civil & Environmental Engineering: Dubai Award for Sustainable Transport (DAST) organized by Dubai’s Roads and Transport Authority (RTA): The University of Sharjah Team from the CEE Department including Dr. Waleed Zeiada and Dr. Muamer Abuzwidah along with the exceptional efforts of students Sham Marwan Miro, Ayat Jamal Ashour, and Reem Nassif Hassan won the first place of the Dubai Award for Sustainable Transport under the Best Academic Research’ Award domain. This year, RTA received 168 applications from the UAE and the MENA region. The submitted research tackled the critical impacts of climate change on the performance grading of asphalt binder, and consequent impacts on long-term performance, life-cycle cost analysis, and CO2 emissions of flexible pavements. This pioneering research, funded by the Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, stands out as the first of its kind in the GCC and MENA regions, aiming to guide future sustainable practices in regions severely impacted by global warming to assure resilient road network.

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter: Electrical-Engineering: EE Department Seminar: Dr. Muhammad Mubasshir Shaikh of the EE Department, gave a seminar titled “Modelling Solar-Terrestrial Interaction Impacting Radio Wave Propagation in Near-Earth Environment”. The talk explored how space weather impacts our radio communication between space and the ground, what factors most affect this scenario and how do we measure or model these effects to improve the reliable usage of our technology in space.

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter:Industrial Engineering and Engineering Management:Dr Zehra Canan Araci: Participated in the Design Thinking Workshop:  Dr Zehra Canan Araci participated in the Design Thinking Workshop which HH Sheikh Mohammad Faisal Al-Qasimi organised in collaboration with the Lean Analytics Association on 17 February 2024. This workshop applied Design Thinking Methodology, a non-linear, iterative process that fosters team collaboration in discovering user needs, redefining problems, and creating innovative prototypes. The workshop addressed two key challenges: 1. Ensuring excellence in innovation across research organisations in the Arabic Gulf region. 2. Transferring knowledge to the commercial, governmental, and third sectors builds a resilient culture for effectively solving society 's strategic issues

COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING news latter:Industrial Engineering and Engineering Management: Design Thinking Workshop by HH Sheikh Mohammad Faisal Al-Qasimi in collaboration with the Lean Analytics Association:  In this workshop, participants applied Design Thinking Methodology, a non-linear, iterative process for teams to discover user needs, understand challenges, redefine problems, and ideate and create innovative prototypes collaboratively. Two challenges are addressed in this workshop: 1. How can we ensure the excellence of innovation in research and technology in research organizations (universities, research centers, companies) in the Arabic Gulf region? 2. How can we transfer knowledge to the commercial, governmental and third sectors, building a resilient culture towards solving society 's strategic issues for the future in an optimal way?

College of Engineering Selected:Students Senior Design Projects Exhibition Catalog May 2024 pdf link : https://www.sharjah.ac.ae/-/media/project/uos/sites/uos/colleges/engineering/highlights/eng_students-design-projects-may2024.pdf 
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Abstract: Disruption of the circadian rhythm contributes to obesity. This study tested whether time-restricted feeding (TRF) reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet. Male C57BL/6 mice were fed either an AIN93G diet or a high-fat diet ad libitum (ad lib), or with the high-fat diet restricted to 12 or 8 hours during the dark cycle. Energy intake of the TRF 12-hour group was similar to the high-fat ad lib group, while the TRF 8-hour group had slightly lower intake. Both TRF groups showed reduced body fat mass and body weight compared to mice fed the high-fat diet ad lib. No differences in respiratory exchange ratio (RER) were found among TRF and high-fat ad lib groups, though all had lower RER than the AIN93G group. Energy expenditure was slightly lower in TRF groups. Plasma ghrelin increased in TRF groups compared to both control groups. High-fat diet-induced elevations in insulin, leptin, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1, and tissue inhibitor metalloproteinase-1 were reduced by TRF to levels similar to mice fed the AIN93G diet. Time-restricted feeding during the dark cycle reduces high-fat diet-induced increases in adiposity and inflammatory markers, suggesting that timing of food intake may prevent obesity and related metabolic disturbances.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Introduction: All mammals exhibit circadian rhythms in daily functions. Energy homeostasis requires coordination of daily rhythms in rest, activity, feeding behavior, energy utilization, and energy storage over the light/dark cycle. Disruption of circadian rhythm by eating at the "wrong" time may disrupt energy homeostasis and promote obesity. Chronic overeating during inappropriate times is often observed in obese humans, leading to metabolic syndrome. Laboratory rodents fed high-fat diets typically lose circadian rhythm, increase food intake, and develop greater body fat mass.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Energy homeostasis regulation involves both adipose tissue and brain. Adipose tissue mediates long-term energy storage and signals the brain regarding whole-body energy status. Circadian rhythm disruption enhances obesity development and metabolic syndrome. Adipokines (leptin, adiponectin) and nutrient-sensitive hormones (ghrelin, insulin) exhibit circadian rhythm-dependent secretory patterns. Temporal disruption of cellular metabolic processes controlled by adipokines predisposes organisms to obesity and related diseases. Obesity worsens adipose tissue dysfunction and increases proinflammatory cytokine secretion, leading to chronic inflammation and angiogenesis that contributes to systemic metabolic disorders.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Current obesity interventions focus on reducing energy intake and increasing physical activity. Intermittent fasting, involving complete or partial food restriction several days weekly, is one approach. Time-restricted feeding (TRF) is another form of intermittent fasting where energy intake is limited to specific hours daily. Previous studies showed that restricted feeding of high-fat diets during the light cycle reduced body weight despite similar caloric intake to ad libitum feeding. Restricted feeding during the dark cycle also reduced body weight, fat mass, and metabolic disturbance markers in non-obese mice. However, TRF's potential to reduce adiposity in obese mice remains unexplored.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: This study tested whether TRF reduces high-fat diet-induced adiposity by applying restricted feeding during the dark cycle (the active phase for nocturnal animals) to mice already showing significant weight increases from high-fat diet consumption.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Methods: Animals and diets: Three-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were maintained in a pathogen-free room on a 12:12-hour light/dark cycle at 22 ± 1°C. Two powder diets were used: AIN93G diet (16% energy from corn oil) and a modified AIN93G diet (45% energy from corn oil, high-fat diet).
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Methods: Experimental design: After one week of acclimation with the AIN93G diet, mice were randomly assigned to receive either AIN93G (n=12) or high-fat diet (n=36) ad libitum. When significant body weight differences emerged (2 weeks later), the high-fat diet mice were divided into three groups: (1) continued ad libitum feeding, (2) 12-hour restricted feeding during the dark cycle, and (3) 8-hour restricted feeding during the dark cycle. Food access for TRF groups was controlled by transferring mice between cages with and without food. Food intake was recorded 5 days weekly for 5 consecutive weeks. Body composition was analyzed by quantitative magnetic resonance imaging one week before study termination.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Methods: Metabolic measurements:  Whole-body metabolic status was evaluated by indirect calorimetry 8 weeks after restricted feeding began. After 24-hour acclimation, activity level, oxygen consumption, and carbon dioxide production were measured for 48 hours. Respiratory exchange ratio and energy expenditure were calculated.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Methods:: Plasma measurements: Sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays quantified plasma concentrations of ghrelin, insulin, adipokines (leptin, adiponectin, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Results: Body weight, composition, and energy intake: High-fat diet increased body weight compared to AIN93G diet within 2 weeks. TRF groups showed lower body weights than high-fat ad lib mice starting 3-7 weeks after restricted feeding began. High-fat ad lib feeding increased body fat percentage and reduced lean mass percentage compared to AIN93G. Both TRF regimens reduced body fat percentage and increased lean mass percentage compared to high-fat ad lib. Energy intake of the 12-hour TRF group matched the high-fat ad lib group, while the 8-hour TRF group consumed approximately 8% less energy.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Results: Metabolic measurements: The respiratory exchange ratio was higher in AIN93G-fed mice (0.92) than all high-fat diet groups (approximately 10% lower), indicating greater carbohydrate oxidation in AIN93G mice versus fat oxidation in high-fat diet mice. High-fat diet reduced oxygen consumption by 15% compared to AIN93G diet. TRF slightly elevated oxygen consumption. No significant differences in ambulatory activity were observed among groups. Energy expenditure was similar between AIN93G and high-fat ad lib groups, but approximately 10% lower in TRF groups.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Results: Plasma markers: Ghrelin increased dose-dependently in TRF groups compared to high-fat ad lib. High-fat diet increased insulin by 39% compared to AIN93G; TRF reduced insulin by 18-24%. Leptin increased 2.4-fold with high-fat diet and decreased 53-63% with TRF. Adiponectin decreased 24% with high-fat diet; 8-hour TRF significantly increased adiponectin. MCP-1 increased 58% with high-fat diet and decreased 31-35% with TRF. TIMP-1 was 28% higher with high-fat diet (non-significant); TRF reduced TIMP-1 by approximately 25%.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Discussion: This study demonstrated that time-restricted feeding of high-fat diet during the dark cycle reduced body adiposity and weight in mice despite similar energy intake to ad libitum feeding. TRF improved diurnal rhythms of RER oscillation between feeding and fasting cycles. Reduced energy expenditure in TRF mice suggests energy conservation during fasting periods, possibly due to metabolic adaptation.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Discussion: Elevated plasma ghrelin in TRF mice indicates a fasting state and chronic negative energy balance. TRF reduced plasma leptin and insulin levels while increasing adiponectin, suggesting improved metabolic regulation. Reductions in proinflammatory MCP-1 and angiogenic factor TIMP-1 with TRF indicate decreased adipose inflammation and angiogenesis, which normally contribute to obesity progression.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: Discussion: Both 12-hour and 8-hour TRF produced similar benefits, though the 8-hour group consumed approximately 11% less energy, suggesting that fasting beyond 12 hours daily might restrict nutrients needed for optimal growth. These results indicate that ad libitum consumption of high-fat diet, not merely fat content, disrupts diurnal feeding rhythm and promotes excessive fat gain. TRF appears to reset metabolic rhythms and reduce inflammation associated with adipogenesis.
Time-restricted feeding reduces adiposity in mice fed a high-fat diet: In conclusion, time-restricted feeding during the dark cycle reduced high-fat diet-induced adiposity in mice that had already gained significant weight. TRF also decreased proinflammatory and angiogenic factors associated with adipogenesis. These findings support the concept that circadian timing of food intake influences obesity development and suggest that TRF may be a promising approach for obesity prevention and treatment
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss artical link: https://www.sharjah.ac.ae/-/media/project/uos/sites/uos/colleges/medicine/highlights/clinical-article.pdf
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Authors Deying Liu, Yan Huang, Chensihan Huang, Shunyu Yang, Xueyun Wei, Peizhen Zhang, Dan Guo, Jiayang Lin, Bingyan Xu, Changwei Li, Hua He, Jiang He, Shiqun Liu, Linna Shi, Yaoming Xue, Huijie Zhang
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Publication Information: The New England Journal of Medicine, April 21, 2022, vol. 386, no. 16, pages 1495-1504
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Abstract: BACKGROUND: The long-term efficacy and safety of time-restricted eating for weight loss are not clear.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: METHODS: We randomly assigned 139 patients with obesity to time-restricted eating (eating only between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.) with calorie restriction or daily calorie restriction alone. For 12 months, all the participants were instructed to follow a calorie-restricted diet that consisted of 1500 to 1800 kcal per day for men and 1200 to 1500 kcal per day for women. The primary outcome was the difference between the two groups in the change from baseline in body weight; secondary outcomes included changes in waist circumference, body-mass index (BMI), amount of body fat, and measures of metabolic risk factors.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: RESULTS: Of the total 139 participants who underwent randomization, 118 (84.9%) completed the 12-month follow-up visit. The mean weight loss from baseline at 12 months was −8.0 kg (95% confidence interval [CI], −9.6 to −6.4) in the time-restriction group and −6.3 kg (95% CI, −7.8 to −4.7) in the daily-calorie-restriction group. Changes in weight were not significantly different in the two groups at the 12-month assessment (net difference, −1.8 kg; 95% CI, −4.0 to 0.4; P = 0.11). Results of analyses of waist circumferences, BMI, body fat, body lean mass, blood pressure, and metabolic risk factors were consistent with the results of the primary outcome. In addition, there were no substantial differences between the groups in the numbers of adverse events.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with obesity, a regimen of time-restricted eating was not more beneficial with regard to reduction in body weight, body fat, or metabolic risk factors than daily calorie restriction.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Obesity is a major global public health challenge.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Weight loss by means of lifestyle modification has been documented to be the cornerstone of weight management.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Daily calorie restriction is a well-established primary weight-loss strategy for obese patients.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Most trials of dietary approaches to weight loss have reported modest (<5%) mean weight loss after 12 months.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Long-term maintenance of weight loss remains a challenge.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Identification of alternative and feasible dietary interventions for weight loss is a major public health priority.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: Time-restricted eating is an intermittent-fasting regimen that involves a shortened period of time for eating within each 24-hour period.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Background: The method has gained popularity because it is a weight-loss strategy that is simple to follow, which may enhance adherence.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Trial Design: Eligible trial participants in Guangzhou, China, were randomly assigned to either a time-restricted eating regimen or a daily-calorie-restriction regimen for 12 months.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Trial Design: The trial was overseen by a steering committee.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Trial Design: The protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Nanfang Hospital of Southern Medical University.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Participants: Total of 139 patients with obesity were recruited.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Participants: Participants were eligible if they were 18 to 75 years of age and had a BMI between 28 and 45
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Participants: Exclusion criteria included acute or chronic viral hepatitis, malignant tumors, diabetes, serious liver dysfunction or chronic kidney disease, current smoking, serious cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease within 6 months before randomization, severe gastrointestinal diseases or gastrointestinal surgery in the 12 months before randomization, active participation in a weight-loss program, use of medications that affect weight or energy balance, and current or planned pregnancy.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Innervention Programs: During the 12 months of the trial, men were instructed to follow a diet of 1500 to 1800 kcal per day and women to follow a diet of 1200 to 1500 kcal per day.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Both diets included a combination of 40 to 55% of calories from carbohydrates, 15 to 20% from protein, and 20 to 30% from fat.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: This regimen represented approximately 75% of the participants' daily caloric intake at baseline.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Participants were provided with one protein shake per day for the first 6 months to help improve adherence.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Time-restricted eating group: instructed to consume the prescribed calories within an 8-hour period (from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.) each day.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Daily-calorie-restriction group: instructed to consume the prescribed calories without time restriction.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Dietary counseling was conducted by trained health coaches.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Intervention Programs: Adherence to the dietary program was defined according to the number of days that a participant met the requirements of the assigned diet.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Primary outcome: difference between the two groups in the change from baseline in body weight at 12 months.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Secondary outcomes: changes in waist circumference, body fat, body lean mass, and metabolic risk factors.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Body fat mass and lean mass were quantified with whole-body dual radiography.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Abdominal visceral fat and subcutaneous fat were obtained by computed tomography.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Liver fat was assessed with transient elastography.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Metabolic risk factors were measured using standard methods.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Insulin-resistance status was measured using the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Outcomes and Measurements: Quality of life was measured according to the 12-item Short-Form Health Survey Questionnaire (SF-12).
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Participant Characteristics: The mean age of the participants was 31.9±9.1 years.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Participant Characteristics: The mean weight was 88.2±11.6 kg.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Participant Characteristics: Physical activity was similar in the two groups over the 12 months of the trial.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Adherence and Calorie Intake: Mean percentage of days that participants adhered to both prescribed calories and eating period: 84.0±16.1% in the time-restricted eating group and 83.8±12.6% in the daily-calorie-restriction group.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Adherence and Calorie Intake: Average caloric deficit and percentages of caloric intake from fats, carbohydrates, and protein were similar in the two groups over 12 months.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Adherence and Calorie Intake: SF-12 physical and mental components scores were similar in the two groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Weight Loss: Mean weight change from baseline to 12 months: −8.0 kg (95% CI, −9.6 to −6.4) in the time-restricted eating group and −6.3 kg (95% CI, −7.8 to −4.7) in the daily-calorie-restriction group.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Weight Loss: No significant difference between the groups in weight change (net difference, −1.8 kg; 95% CI, −4.0 to 0.4; P = 0.11).
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Weight Loss: Percentages of participants with weight loss of more than 5%, 10%, and 15% at 12 months were similar in the two groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Weight Loss: Weight changes were similar for the two regimens across all subgroups (sex, BMI at baseline, insulin sensitivity, and adherence to the prescribed diet).
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Weight Loss: Similar reductions from baseline in waist circumference and BMI in both groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Body Composition: Body fat mass at 12 months was reduced by 5.9 kg (95% CI, −7.1 to −4.7) from baseline in the time-restricted eating group and by 4.5 kg (95% CI, −5.6 to −3.3) in the daily-calorie-restriction group, with no substantial differences between the groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Body Composition: Both dietary approaches led to similar losses of lean mass, abdominal visceral fat, subcutaneous fat, and liver fat.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Blood Pressure, Lipids, Glucose, and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors: Both time-restricted eating and daily calorie restriction were associated with reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure over 12 months, with no substantial between-group differences.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Blood Pressure, Lipids, Glucose, and Cardiometabolic Risk Factors: Fasting glucose levels, 2-hour postprandial glucose levels, scores on the insulin disposition index and HOMA-IR, and lipid levels were similar in the two groups during the 12 months of the trial.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Adverse Events: No deaths or serious adverse events were reported during the trial.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Adverse Events: Occurrences of mild adverse events, such as fatigue, dizziness, headache, decreased appetite, upper abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and constipation, were similar in the two groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: The 8-hour time-restricted eating regimen did not produce greater weight loss than the regimen of daily calorie restriction, with both regimens resulting in similar caloric deficits.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: Time-restricted eating and daily calorie restriction produced similar effects with respect to reductions in body fat, visceral fat, blood pressure, glucose levels, and lipid levels over the 12-month intervention period.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: These results indicate that caloric intake restriction explained most of the beneficial effects seen with the time-restricted eating regimen.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: The time-restricted eating regimen worked as an alternative option for weight management.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: The time period from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. was selected because many Chinese people eat their biggest meal in the middle of the day rather than in the evening.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: Both dieting regimens had similar efficacy in reducing the levels of body fat and visceral fat from baseline in obese patients.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: No significant differences between the groups in gains in body lean mass over the 12-month intervention period.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: The findings indicate the importance of a balanced diet and adequate protein consumption in patients who are adhering to a diet regimen of time-restricted eating.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: Time-restricted eating did not provide additional benefits with regard to blood pressure as compared with daily calorie restriction.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Key Findings and Discussion: Participants in both diet groups had improvement in glucose and lipid levels and in HOMA-IR index values, with no differences between the groups.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Clinical Implications: Among patients with obesity, a regimen of time-restricted eating was not more beneficial with regard to reduction in body weight, body fat, or metabolic risk factors than daily calorie restriction.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Clinical Implications: Caloric intake restriction explained most of the beneficial effects of a time-restricted eating regimen.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Clinical Implications: Time-restricted eating combined with caloric intake restriction represents a viable and sustainable approach for obesity management.
Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss: Study Information: Results: Clinical Implications: The findings could not be generalized to patients with diabetes or cardiovascular disease, to different periods of time-restricted eating, or to persons of other races or ethnic groups.
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: AUTHORS: Tom Y. Chang, Agne Kajackaite
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: PUBLICATION: PLOS ONE, May 22, 2019
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: ABSTRACT: This paper studies differences in the effect of temperature on cognitive performance by gender in a large controlled lab experiment (N = 543). Performance was measured in math, verbal and cognitive reflection tasks. The effects of temperature vary significantly across men and women. At higher temperatures, women perform better on math and verbal tasks while the reverse effect is observed for men. The increase in female performance in response to higher temperature is significantly larger and more precisely estimated than the corresponding decrease in male performance. Temperature has no impact on cognitive reflection for either gender. Findings suggest that gender-mixed workplaces may increase productivity by setting thermostat higher than current standards.
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: KEY FINDINGS: - Women perform better at math and verbal tasks at higher temperatures - Men perform better at math and verbal tasks at lower temperatures - For women, a 1°C increase in temperature is associated with 1.76% increase in math questions correctly answered - For men, a 1°C increase in temperature is associated with 0.63% decrease in correct math answers - For verbal tasks, 1°C temperature increase improves female performance by 1.03% and decreases male performance by 0.6% - Temperature had no significant effect on Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) scores for either gender - Women attempt more questions at higher temperatures; men attempt fewer
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: METHODOLOGY:- 543 participants (41.14% female) in Berlin, Germany- Temperature varied between 16.19-32.57°C across different sessions- Tasks: math (adding five two-digit numbers), verbal (building German words from letters), and cognitive reflection test- Between-subject design with varying temperatures across sessions- Temperature ranges: <20°C, 20-25°C, 25-30°C, >30°C- All tasks were monetarily incentivized based on performance
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: IMPLICATIONS: - Gender is important in determining temperature effects on productivity and cognitive performance - Results may explain inconsistent findings in previous studies on temperature and performance - In gender-balanced workplaces, setting temperatures higher than current standards may optimize overall productivity - The study contributes to literature on gender differences in performance and workplace conditions
Battle for the thermostat: Gender and the effect of temperature on cognitive performance: SUMMARY: Study of 543 participants showing temperature affects cognitive performance differently by gender. Women perform better at math and verbal tasks in warmer temperatures (1°C increase = 1.76% improvement in math); men perform better in cooler environments. Temperature had no effect on cognitive reflection tests. Results suggest higher office temperatures may optimize productivity in gender-mixed workplaces.

Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Overview: The Medical Students Research Subcommittee (MSRS), established in the academic year 2020/2021 at the College of Medicine, University of Sharjah, focuses on supporting and empowering medical students in the field of research, both in basic and clinical biomedical research. It aims to create a platform that fosters scientific collaboration between students and faculty while promoting research initiatives.
Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Vision: . Empower students to engage in both basic and clinical medical research. . Create an environment conducive to faculty and students interested in biomedical research. . Foster strong scientific relationships between students and faculty.
Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Aims: . Create a platform for fostering scientific relationships between faculty and students. . Disseminate research activities among medical students. . Empower students in research through educational methods. . Organize activities to encourage students to present their research findings.
Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Mission: . The subcommittee’s primary mission is to: . Educate students on conducting basic and clinical research. . Organize training workshops on various aspects of research, including: Study design, Proposal writing and Finalizing research for publication. . Support student research projects by helping identify funding resources. . Organize seminars and conferences to showcase students' research.
Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Key Activities: . Intro Session: A session designed to introduce students to the program, its goals, and activities. . Journal Clubs: Discussions on clinical and lab articles. . Workshops: Two parts on how to write a research manuscript:Part I: Focus on the basics of writing a research manuscript, Part II: More advanced writing skills.
Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Members: . Chairperson: Dr. Noha Mousa . Co-Chair: Prof. Mohamed Saleh . Other Members: Professors and Doctors from various fields within the College of Medicine. . Student Representatives:Mazen Alhaj Ahmad (Clinical Phase) and Lamees Amir Mohamedali (Pre-Clinical Phase)

Medical Students Research Program (MSRP): Summary: The Medical Students Research Program (MSRP) provides students with ample opportunities to enhance their research skills through workshops, journal clubs, and support for student-led research initiatives. It serves as a valuable resource for students to integrate their academic knowledge into practical research and contribute to the scientific community.

Foreword by Khalid Seddiq Al Motawea: Etihad Modern Art Gallery is honored to host the Annual Faculty Show of the College of Fine Arts and Design, University of Sharjah. The exhibit includes work of distinguished fine arts students and aims to bring contemporary arts closer to audiences. The exhibition features a diverse range of cultural backgrounds and art mediums including drawing, painting, photography, printmaking, calligraphy, graphic design, sculpture, and digital art.
Theme Introduction by Nadia M. Alhasani: The exhibition theme "Yearning" explores reactions to our fast-paced digital world. Artists express a desire to slow down and reflect on personal memories. The works capture fleeting moments and invite viewers to contemplate the artists' yearning for people or things from the past. The exhibition celebrates the diverse creative skills of faculty, staff, and students.
